name: Magnesite
physical: Kept nearby for comfort during stressful times
Crystal healers link it to easing muscle tension and restful sleep
summary: Magnesite is a cool, chalky white or grey carbonate, often dyed turquoise, used in crystal tradition for relaxation, patience and stress relief.
intro: Magnesite is a magnesium carbonate that occurs as dense white to pale grey masses, often with delicate grey veins that give it a marble-like pattern. It is naturally matte and chalky, with a soft, creamy look. Because it is porous it takes dye readily, and bright turquoise-colored magnesite beads flood the market as an inexpensive imitation of the real thing. Natural white pieces are quiet and elegant. In the crystal tradition magnesite is known as a mellow, relaxing stone, helpful for people who feel pushed to their limits by pressure and perfectionism.
history: The name comes from the region of Magnesia in Greece, where the mineral was historically found, and it shares that root with magnesium and magnet. Magnesite has long been mined for refractory bricks, which line furnaces, and as a source of magnesium. White magnesite nodules also became a common gem material in the twentieth century, mainly for beads. Its dyed blue form was developed as a cheap alternative to turquoise. Magnesite has no historical metaphysical tradition, and its reputation as a calming stone is modern.
meaning: Crystal healers describe magnesite as a stone that eases tension and encourages patience. It is associated with the crown and heart chakras and used to quiet a restless mind, particularly in people who fixate on details or push themselves too hard. Practitioners say it promotes tolerance and the ability to accept others as they are. It is often used for relaxation before sleep and as a stone for meditation. Emotionally it is said to cool irritability, soften self-criticism and bring a feeling of ease. Traditionally it is also linked to relaxed muscles and gentle, stress-soothing comfort. It is a soft, calm stone rather than a dynamic one, and many keep it near their workspace for steadying energy.
howToUse: Hold a magnesite stone in the palm during breathing exercises, counting slow breaths until the mind quiets. Place one on your desk or by your bed to encourage relaxation. Wear magnesite beads as a bracelet for gentle daily support, taking them off before showers. Add it to a calming grid with howlite and clear quartz. Some people place a piece on the third eye during a short evening meditation, or on the heart for emotional ease.
care: Magnesite is soft and porous, and it reacts to acids, so keep it away from vinegar and strong cleaners. Do not soak it; dyed pieces can lose color in water. Wipe with a dry soft cloth. Cleanse with sound, smoke, breath or moonlight. Keep dyed pieces out of strong sunlight, which can fade them. Store separately to prevent scratches and moisture.
identify: Natural magnesite is white to grey, chalky and fine-grained, sometimes with grey veining, and it will not fizz as quickly in cold acid as calcite. It is easily confused with howlite, which has darker spider-web veining, and with turquoise when dyed. Dyed magnesite shows color concentrated in cracks and may rub off on a cotton swab with acetone. Genuine turquoise is harder and has a waxy luster, with natural brown matrix.

faq.q: Is magnesite the same as howlite?
faq.a: No. Magnesite is a magnesium carbonate, while howlite is a calcium borosilicate. They look similar, since both are white and often dyed, but howlite usually has darker spider-web veining and is slightly softer.
In crystal tradition magnesite is used for relaxation, patience and stress relief. People keep it by the bed, on a desk or as beads to bring a calm, accepting mood.
It is better to avoid water. Magnesite is porous and soft, and dyed pieces can lose color or become dull. Wipe with a soft dry cloth and cleanse with sound, breath or moonlight.
